draft.title: Egypt's legacy
card: Writing
Egyptians used hieroglyphs, a script of picture signs, on temple walls, monuments and papyrus. Scribes also used a faster, simpler script for everyday records.
Monuments
Pyramids, temples and statues still stand today. They show Egyptian skill in building and tell us about their beliefs and rulers.
Maths and medicine
Egyptians used mathematics to measure farm land and plan buildings. Their doctors wrote medical texts on papyrus and treated wounds and illnesses.
Rosetta Stone

For centuries no one could read hieroglyphs. The Rosetta Stone has the same text in three scripts, including Greek, which people could read. In the 1820s Jean-François Champollion used it to decode hieroglyphs, opening Egypt's records to historians.
draft.remember: Egypt's writing, monuments, maths and medicine left evidence, and the Rosetta Stone let historians read it.

a.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so useful for decoding hieroglyphs?
opts: It had the same text in Greek, which could be read
It was the only hieroglyphic text ever written
It was a dictionary of hieroglyphs made by scribes
It was written in a script that was simple to read
a.why: The stone repeats one text in three scripts, and Greek was already understood. This gave a way to work out the hieroglyphs. It was not the only hieroglyphic text, as hieroglyphs cover many monuments and papyri.
a.clue: Think about which script on the stone people could already read.

b.q: A historian in the 1700s could not read the carvings on an Egyptian temple. A historian today can. What changed?
opts: Hieroglyphs were decoded after the 1820s
The carvings were rewritten in modern letters
New temples were built with Greek writing
Egyptians began using a simpler script again
b.why: Champollion decoded hieroglyphs in the 1820s using the Rosetta Stone, so historians could read the old carvings. The carvings were not rewritten: the same signs are read today.
b.clue: Think about the discovery that opened up Egypt's written records.
